text: 胡适自己说，把他推上这条路的，是一连串的小意外：一首送别诗，一场湖上的险事。他一向反对用某一个原因解释所有历史，常开玩笑说，意外往往比那些包打天下的“单因”更重要。他也说，诗集取名《尝试集》，表明他受了美国哲学家杜威“实验主义”的影响：一切理论都只是假设，要靠实际试验来证明或反证。白话在小说、元曲、民歌里已经得到证明，剩下的诗，正是他要用一段试验来检验的部分。

Hu himself said that what pushed him down this road was a chain of small accidents: a farewell poem, a scare on a lake. He distrusted theories that explain all of history by a single cause, and liked to joke that accidents often matter more than any one cause that claims to explain everything. He also said the name of the collection, Experiments, showed the influence of the experimentalism of the American philosopher John Dewey: every theory is only a hypothesis, to be proved or disproved by actual trial. The vernacular had already proved itself in novels, Yuan drama and folk songs; poetry was the part left, the part he proposed to test with an experiment.
作者推断：把诗当作待检验的假设，是胡适自己的说法；从他的做法里还能多看出两点。一是他还没写出几首白话诗，就先给诗集取好名字，等于先替自己定下要举证的任务；二是他在信里先写好了失败的退路，承认这块新地可能是不毛之地，这让它更像一场真正的试验，而不是换个方式继续辩论。发表时他把调子放低，陈独秀随后把旗子举高。

The author's inference: treating poetry as a hypothesis to be tested was Hu's own framing; his conduct shows two things more. First, he named the collection before he had written more than a few vernacular poems, in effect setting himself the task of supplying the proof. Second, in his letters he wrote down his retreat in case of failure, granting that the new land might prove barren — which made it a real experiment rather than the argument continued by other means. When he published, he lowered his voice, and Chen then raised the banner.
这段经过来自胡适晚年的口述回忆（唐德刚译注）：事件见原书第七章，结局见第八章；朋友们的话都经他转述。标明“作者推断”的段落是本文的解读，唐德刚的评语另作评论看待。详细说明见文末“出处与不确定性”。

This account comes from Hu's oral memoir, given late in life and translated and annotated by Tang Degang: the events are in chapter 7 of the book, the outcome in chapter 8; his friends' words all reach us through Hu. Paragraphs marked as the author's inference are this article's reading, and Tang's remarks are treated as commentary. More under Sources and uncertainty at the end.

本文只依据一本书：胡适口述、唐德刚译注《胡适口述自传》（中国文史出版社，2020）。事件经过出自第七章《文学革命的结胎时期》，结局（1920年教育部通令、“部分的胜利”）出自第八章《从文学革命到文艺复兴》，两章都是当事人多年后的口述回忆。按唐德刚在第七章注释里的说明，第七章的英文稿是从胡适《四十自述》的《逼上梁山》一章节译、经胡适手订后再回译成中文的，与原文多少有出入；这一说明只针对第七章。第七章引述了他1916年7月6日的日记和7月26日致任鸿隽的信等当时文字，但本文依据的只是经胡适转引、再经英译与回译的文本，未核对原件。梅光迪、任鸿隽的言行都经胡适转述；胡适对“改良”措辞的解释是他事后的说法。唐德刚在第七章的注释属评论：他认为“文言是半死的文字”这句口号当年摧枯拉朽，但真实性值得重新商榷；他认为白话文百分之百成功，白话诗则还未脱离“尝试”阶段；他也记下反对者觉得胡适居功太多，1956年胡适在哈佛以此讲演时，后来为他作传的格里德嗤之以鼻。这些都是唐德刚的记述，本文未另行核验。关于白话诗的结果，胡适本人在第八章则说「四十年来的新诗更是大有成就」，同时承认新文学各部门发展并不平均。标为“作者推断”的段落是本文的解读，思考题中的场景是虚构的。

This piece rests on one book: Hu Shi's oral memoir, translated and annotated by Tang Degang (Chinese Literature and History Press, 2020). The events come from chapter 7, The Gestation of the Literary Revolution; the outcome (the 1920 Ministry of Education order, the partial victory) from chapter 8, From Literary Revolution to Renaissance. Both chapters are a participant's oral recollection many years later. As Tang explains in a note to chapter 7, the English draft of that chapter was abridged from the Driven to Liangshan chapter of Hu's Forty Self-Narratives, revised in Hu's own hand and then translated back into Chinese, and it differs from the original to some degree; this applies to chapter 7 only. Chapter 7 quotes writings from the time, such as Hu's diary entry of July 6, 1916 and his letter to Ren Hongjun of July 26. This article relies only on those texts as Hu quoted them, then translated into English and back again, and has not checked the originals. Mei Guangdi's and Ren Hongjun's words and actions reach us through Hu, and his explanation of the moderate wording is his own later account. Tang's notes to chapter 7 are commentary: he thought the slogan that the classical language is half dead was devastating in its day but that its truth deserves a fresh look; he judged vernacular prose a complete success and vernacular poetry not yet out of the experimental stage; and he records that Hu's opponents felt he claimed too much credit, and that when Hu gave this account in a 1956 lecture at Harvard, Jerome B. Grieder, later his biographer, scoffed. These are Tang's accounts and were not checked separately here. On the outcome for vernacular poetry, Hu himself says in chapter 8 that the new poetry of the past forty years had achieved a great deal, while acknowledging that the different branches of the new literature developed unevenly. Paragraphs marked as the author's inference are this article's reading; the scenario in the question is fictional.
